Phuu Thit Kyaw

Climate adaptation researcher

Phuu Thit Kyaw is a climate adaptation researcher with an MSc in Climate Studies from Wageningen University & Research and a background in river and coastal engineering. Her work connects research and decision-making: assessing climate risk and vulnerability, designing adaptation pathways, and working with communities and governments to plan for uncertain futures. She currently supports regional and global adaptation initiatives at PlanAdapt under the UK–Canada CLARE research programme.

2025

MSc thesis at Deltares and WUR

Integrating equity into adaptation pathways: the EADP framework

Wageningen University & Research, in partnership with Deltares

A seven-step framework that builds fairness into climate adaptation planning. Impacts, goals, thresholds and pathways are worked out for each stakeholder group, and outcomes are checked for equity. Built from three systematic literature reviews and refined through interviews with ten experts, with a hypothetical Mekong Delta example.

  • Distributive justice

2024 – 2025

MSc internship at Deltares

Towards a climate-resilient Logroño, Spain

Deltares, EU Horizon REACHOUT project

Co-developed Climate Resilient Development Pathways (CRDPs) for Logroño, a city of over 150,000 people in northern Spain facing heatwaves, floods and droughts. The city had impact analyses for heat, flooding and social vulnerability, and wanted to move from those to action planning. The pathways combine adaptation, mitigation and sustainable development over time and under uncertainty.

  • GIS hotspot mapping
  • Climate scenarios
  • Interaction analysis
  • Multi-criteria analysis
  • Pathways design
  • Stakeholder co-development

Supervised by Dr. Gaby S. Langendijk (Deltares) and Dr. Raffaele Vignola (WUR). Partners: Tecnalia Research & Innovation and Ayuntamiento de Logroño.

Explore the project
7 stepsin the CRDP approach; this project did the first four
3 futuresenvisioned with the city and partners
46 measuresscored in the multi-criteria analysis
Bi-weeklymeetings presented and moderated with partners

Step 1Map the decision context

Combined the REACHOUT tools' land surface temperature maps, simulated pluvial flood depths and social vulnerability index maps in GIS to find hotspots. About 36,800 people live where extreme heat meets high social vulnerability, and about 32,900 where heat and pluvial flooding overlap. Seven city plans and policies were reviewed to set goals for mitigation, adaptation and sustainable development.

Goals set with the city. Mitigation: a 55% cut in CO₂-equivalent emissions by 2030. Adaptation: reduce damage and people exposed to floods, heatwaves and droughts. Sustainable development: more urban biodiversity, and health and well-being for all residents.

Step 2Envision futures and define strategies

Three futures were developed together with Tecnalia and the Logroño City Council.

Future 1: Compact Growth & Resilience

Reuse existing space and avoid urban sprawl. Only the measures already planned are implemented, so climate action may fall short.

Future 2: Green Growth & Biodiverse

Focus on green measures and tree planting that act as a carbon sink and help against heat, floods and droughts.

Future 3: Integrative & Climate-Proof

Balance adaptation, mitigation and development, adding complementary measures chosen for their co-benefits and synergies.

Step 3Map the solution space

Planned and new measures were checked for co-benefits and trade-offs with ten sub-objectives, and for synergies and conflicts with each other, using literature, C40's AMIA tool and the SCAN tool. A multi-criteria analysis, with criteria and weights agreed with stakeholders, then scored every measure.

Performance 30%Cost 30%Side-effects 20%Technical feasibility 10%Socio-institutional acceptance 10%

Weighted score out of 3; each criterion is scored 1 to 3. Select a measure to see its criterion scores. Appendix C of the report.

When is new action needed? Tipping points from the heat and flood projections of the REACHOUT tools:

Short termNow to 2030–36Prepare for four heatwaves a year, double the current two.
Medium term2030–36 to 2060–65Heatwaves double again to about eight. Flood intensity doubles, so measures must be at least twice as effective.
Long termAfter 2060–65Twelve heatwaves under RCP 4.5, up to thirty-two under RCP 8.5. No flood simulations after 2065.

Step 4Design and evaluate pathways

Pathways were designed for each future under two scenarios: medium decarbonisation with strong socio-economic growth (RCP 4.5), and high emissions with weaker growth (RCP 8.5).

Each future's adaptation measures were scored for heat, flood and drought over three time horizons, using the multi-criteria and interaction results.

Pivotal decisions. Before 2030, new housing, transport infrastructure and parks may compete for the same space. In the medium term, a proposed green corridor needs to be planned alongside transport routes. In the long term, the choice is which hybrid flood measures to combine.

WorkshopPutting the pathways to use

The pathways were presented at the Year 3 REACHOUT workshop in Logroño, where government officials, private sector representatives and citizens used them to co-create pathways for the city. Deltares continues the CRDP process from this work.

LimitsWhat the project could not cover

  • Several steps relied on expert judgement, and the interaction analysis on qualitative literature.
  • Fluvial flooding from the Ebro River and future droughts lacked data, which limited the tipping points.
  • The pathways are an illustrative first application, not final solutions for the city.

2013 – 2019

B.Eng. in River and Coastal Engineering

Analysis of bank erosion in the Pan Hlaing River at Nyaungdon

Bachelor's thesis, Myanmar Maritime University, Yangon

Nyaungdon sits where the Pan Hlaing River splits from the Ayeyarwaddy in southwest Myanmar. Since a navigation channel was dredged in 1986, more water flows into the Pan Hlaing at higher speed, and the town's riverbank has been eroding. The study asked what causes the erosion, and how future bank protection could respond.

  • Hydrographic surveys
  • Velocity and discharge (ADCP)
  • Satellite change detection
  • ArcGIS and QGIS
  • Slope stability (GeoStudio)

Linked to a student internship at Arcadis on bank and bed protection of the Ayeyarwady River at Nyaungdon, using data from the Directorate of Water Resources and Improvement of River Systems (DWIR) and the Irrigation Department (IWUMD).

Explore the study

Slope stability modelling

The bank at 21st street, where slope failures had occurred, was modelled in GeoStudio to find its factor of safety against a circular slip failure. The model used Bishop's method with an entry-and-exit slip surface and a Mohr–Coulomb soil model. Soil layers, cohesion, friction angle and unit weight came from DWIR, and the bank slope was assumed at 1:2. Three water conditions were simulated, then repeated with the revetment being built there, including its materials and piles.

A factor of safety below 1 means the slope fails; the thesis treats values below 1.5 as unstable. The model covers mass failure only, not erosion by the flow, and the effect of the piles was not checked exactly.

What the study found

  • Flow is faster and water deeper along the Nyaungdon bank than elsewhere at the bifurcation, and more water entered the Pan Hlaing in 2017 than in 2016.
  • The river's shape changed: the north bank became the outer bend, with erosion at the outer bend and sediment building up at the inner bend.
  • The bank mostly fails when water levels drop suddenly after the rainy season or a flood. The revetment raises the safety factor, but only to about 1.5 to 1.7, and its main foundation still sits inside the slip circle, so a larger foundation and toe protection are needed.
  • Soft clay and silt banks, buildings close to the waterfront, and ship waves add to the erosion.

Recommendations

Model mass failure and fluvial erosion together, build 2D or 3D hydraulic models, include seepage and groundwater, and assess Nyaungdon's flood risk if the protective sand bar moves away.
